summary: This note describes the provinces and territories of Canada as the administrative divisions that deliver sub-national governance under the Canadian Constitution. It traces how the 1867 Confederation united New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the Province of Canada, which was then split into Ontario and Quebec, and how the country grew to ten provinces and three territories. It also notes the historical colonial origins of several provinces and that together these divisions make Canada the world's second-largest country by area.
one_line: Overview of Canada's ten provinces and three territories, their origins in the 1867 Confederation, and their role in sub-national governance.
key_facts: The provinces and territories of Canada are the administrative divisions responsible for sub-national governance under the Canadian Constitution.
In the 1867 Canadian Confederation, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and the Province of Canada were united to form a federated colony.
Upon Confederation, the Province of Canada was divided into Ontario and Quebec.
The federated colony formed in 1867 eventually became a sovereign nation in the next century.
Canada grew from the original four provinces to the current ten provinces and three territories.
The ten provinces are Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, and Saskatchewan.
Several of the provinces were former British colonies.
Quebec was originally a French colony.
The three territories are Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Yukon.
The territories govern the rest of the area of the former British North America.
Canada's international borders have changed several times over its history.
Together, the provinces and territories make up the world's second-largest country by area.
